subject: Science (Physics)
summary: In-depth study of electrical circuits, standardized circuit symbols, cell polarity, battery combinations, the Joule heating effect (H = I²Rt) in appliances, electrical safety mechanisms (fuse wires, MCBs, earthing), and Hans Christian Oersted's discovery of the magnetic effect of electric current powering electromagnets, electric bells, relays, and industrial scrap lifters.

theory_summary.content: An electric circuit is a continuous, unbroken conducting loop through which electric current flows from the positive terminal of an electric energy source (cell or battery), through conducting wires and control switches, to an electrical load (bulb, resistor), and returns to the negative terminal. Standard circuit symbols: 1. Connecting Wire: Straight solid line. 2. Electric Cell: Two parallel vertical lines — the longer, thinner line represents the Positive (+) terminal, while the shorter, thicker line represents the Negative (−) terminal. 3. Battery: A series combination of two or more cells where the positive terminal of one cell connects to the negative terminal of the next. 4. Switch (Key): Represented with an open gap (OFF position — circuit broken, zero current) or a bridged line (ON position — closed continuous circuit). 5. Electric Bulb: A circle with a central curled filament loop.

theory_summary.topic: Heating Effect of Electric Current & Joule's Law
theory_summary.content: When electric current flows through a conductor having electrical resistance (R), moving electrons collide with the fixed lattice atoms, transferring kinetic energy that dissipates as heat. Formulated by James Prescott Joule, the heat produced is: H = I²Rt (where I is current in amperes, R is resistance in ohms, and t is time in seconds). Appliances utilizing this effect (room heaters, electric toasters, geysers, hair dryers, immersion rods, and electric irons) contain heating elements made of high-resistivity, high-melting-point alloys like Nichrome (Nickel + Chromium + Iron). Incandescent bulbs contain an ultra-thin tungsten filament heated to white-hot glow (~2500°C) encased in an inert gas (Argon/Nitrogen) atmosphere to prevent oxidation.

theory_summary.topic: Safety Devices: Electric Fuses, MCBs & Earthing
theory_summary.content: Overloading (connecting too many high-power appliances to a single socket) or Short-Circuiting (direct contact between live and neutral wires due to damaged insulation) causes excessive, dangerously high currents that can spark fires. 1. Electric Fuse: A sacrificial safety device placed in the live wire containing a thin wire made of an alloy of Lead (Pb) and Tin (Sn) possessing a low melting point. If current exceeds the rated threshold (e.g. 5A or 15A), Joule heating immediately melts the fuse wire, breaking the circuit. Fuses must never be replaced by thick copper wires. 2. Miniature Circuit Breakers (MCBs): Modern electromagnetic/bimetallic automatic switches that trip and flip downward to the OFF position within milliseconds during overcurrent. They are safer and easily reset manually once the fault is cleared without wire replacement. 3. Earthing: A third low-resistance ground wire conducting leakage current safely into the Earth, protecting users from lethal shocks.

Discovered by Danish physicist Hans Christian Oersted in 1820: when electric current passes through a conducting wire, it produces an invisible magnetic field in its surrounding space, causing a nearby magnetic compass needle to deflect. An Electromagnet consists of an insulated copper wire tightly coiled into a solenoid around a core of magnetic material (soft iron). It acts as a powerful magnet only when current is flowing and loses its magnetism almost instantaneously when switched off (temporary magnet). Strength of an electromagnet increases with: (a) increasing number of coil turns, (b) increasing electric current, and (c) using a high-permeability soft iron core. Key applications: heavy scrap-metal cranes, electric bells, magnetic levitation (Maglev) bullet trains, relays, loudspeakers, MRI medical imaging, and extracting magnetic iron splinters from a patient's eye.

questions.question: The torch bulb is connected to the cell with the help of:
questions.explanation: To form a complete, closed circuit allowing current to flow from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb filament, and back to the other terminal, two connecting wires are required.

questions.question: What type of energy conversion happens in a cell when it powers a torch?
questions.explanation: An electric cell contains chemicals that undergo redox reactions, transforming chemical potential energy directly into electrical energy.

questions.question: What is the source of electricity in a typical portable torch?
questions.explanation: The electric cells (or battery of cells) act as the chemical source of electromotive force (voltage) driving the current in a portable torch.

questions.question: If a torch does not work even when switched on, which of the following could be the reason?
options: (b) The cells are not connected properly (wrong polarity)
(c) The metal parts do not make proper contact
questions.explanation: Any discontinuity or reversal of cells prevents a closed circuit, causing the torch to fail to light.

questions.question: Sometimes an electric bulb does not glow even when connected to a cell without any visible gap. This can occur due to:
questions.explanation: A broken filament breaks the internal path; an exhausted cell provides no voltage; loose connections cause infinite resistance.

questions.question: What is the function of a switch in an electric circuit?
options: (c) To control (make or break) the flow of current
(d) To provide energy to the circuit
questions.answer: (c) To control (make or break) the flow of current
questions.explanation: A switch is a control device designed to manually close (complete) or open (break) the conductive path of current.

questions.question: Which of the following components is used to store electrical energy chemically?
questions.explanation: A battery or accumulator stores energy in chemical form and releases it as electrical current during discharge.

questions.question: When an electric switch is in the 'OFF' position: (i) the circuit is broken at the switch, (ii) the circuit is open, (iii) no current flows through it, (iv) current flows after some time. Choose the correct combination:
questions.explanation: In the OFF position, the switch creates an air gap, leaving the circuit open so zero current can flow.

questions.question: A key or switch in an electric circuit can be placed:
options: (a) Only on the left side of the battery
(b) Only on the right side of the battery
(d) Only near the positive terminal of the bulb
questions.explanation: Current flows through a continuous loop. Breaking the loop at any position stops the current throughout the entire series circuit.

questions.question: Which of the following represents the standard circuit symbol of an electric bulb?
options: (a) A circle enclosing a coiled loop or crossed filament
(b) A long and short parallel line
questions.answer: (a) A circle enclosing a coiled loop or crossed filament
questions.explanation: The standard schematic symbol for an incandescent lamp/bulb is a circle with a loop or cross representing the filament.

questions.question: The shorter, thicker vertical line in the symbol of an electric cell represents:
questions.explanation: In standard schematics, the long thin line represents the positive terminal (+), while the short thick line represents the negative terminal (-).

questions.question: Which switch, if opened in a main supply branch, will cause all light bulbs in that circuit branch to stop glowing?
options: (a) The master switch in series with the power source
questions.answer: (a) The master switch in series with the power source
questions.explanation: A master switch placed in the main line controls the entire circuit loop, interrupting the current to all downstream loads.

questions.question: The SI unit of electric charge is the:
questions.explanation: Charge is measured in Coulombs ($Q = I \times t$). Ampere is current, Joule is energy, and Watt is power.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a physical circuit component (element)?
questions.explanation: Potential difference is a physical quantity (measured in volts), whereas resistors, voltmeters, and batteries are physical components/instruments.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a source of electric current?
questions.explanation: An electromagnet is a load that consumes electrical energy to produce magnetic force; it does not generate electric current.

questions.question: Which of the following elements has the highest electrical conductivity at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of all known metals, followed closely by copper and gold.

questions.question: Why is copper wire universally preferred for domestic electrical wiring?
options: (a) Copper is an excellent conductor with high ductility and low cost relative to silver
(c) Copper has high resistance like nichrome
questions.answer: (a) Copper is an excellent conductor with high ductility and low cost relative to silver
questions.explanation: Copper combines high electrical conductivity, excellent mechanical flexibility (ductility), and cost-effectiveness.

questions.question: Electrical conductors are defined as materials that:
options: (a) Allow electric current to pass through them freely
(b) Completely block the flow of electric current
(c) Store charge without letting it move
questions.answer: (a) Allow electric current to pass through them freely
questions.explanation: Conductors have abundant free electrons that drift readily under an applied electric field, allowing current to flow.

questions.question: Among the following metals, which is the best conductor of electricity?
questions.explanation: Silver has the lowest resistivity ($\approx 1.59 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot\text{m}$), making it the best conductor.

questions.question: Why is domestic wiring made of copper rather than silver?
options: (a) Copper is a better conductor than silver
(c) Copper is far less expensive than precious silver
questions.answer: (c) Copper is far less expensive than precious silver
questions.explanation: Silver is a precious metal and prohibitively expensive for large-scale wiring, whereas copper is economical and widely available.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT belong to the group formed by the others?
questions.explanation: A wooden ruler is an electrical insulator, whereas copper coins, steel spoons, and iron nails are electrical conductors.

questions.question: Why are copper electric wires covered with an outer layer of PVC plastic or rubber?
options: (c) To act as electrical insulation and prevent electric shocks and short circuits
questions.answer: (c) To act as electrical insulation and prevent electric shocks and short circuits
questions.explanation: Plastic and rubber are excellent insulators that protect humans from lethal electric shocks and prevent bare wires from touching.

questions.question: Which among the following materials is an electrical insulator?
questions.explanation: Both wool and plastic are non-conductors (insulators) because they lack free mobile charge carriers.

questions.question: In which of the following circuits will identical bulbs glow the brightest?
options: (a) A circuit with one bulb and one cell
(b) A circuit with one bulb and two cells connected in series
(c) A circuit with two bulbs and one cell in series
(d) A circuit with three bulbs and one cell in series
questions.answer: (b) A circuit with one bulb and two cells connected in series
questions.explanation: Connecting two cells in series doubles the voltage ($V = 2E$), driving twice the current through a single bulb ($P = V^2/R$), yielding maximum brightness.

questions.question: In a tester circuit, the bulb does not glow when an unknown object is connected between the test probes. The object is most likely a:
questions.explanation: A rubber eraser is an electrical insulator. It creates an open circuit, preventing current from reaching the bulb.

questions.question: A student connected two bulbs in series with two cells. How can he make the bulbs glow dimmer?
options: (a) Add a third cell in series
(b) Remove one cell and complete the connection with a wire
(c) Replace the connecting wires with thicker copper wire
(d) Add a third bulb in parallel
questions.answer: (b) Remove one cell and complete the connection with a wire
questions.explanation: Removing one cell halves the source electromotive force, reducing current and causing the bulbs to glow dimmer.

questions.question: When connecting a Light Emitting Diode (LED) into a circuit, the longer lead (terminal) must always be connected to the:
options: (d) It can be connected either way
questions.explanation: An LED is a polar semiconductor device. The longer lead is the positive anode and the shorter lead is the negative cathode.

questions.question: In an electrical circuit, what physically happens when the switch is moved to the 'OFF' position?
options: (a) An air gap is introduced, breaking the loop so zero current can flow
(b) The voltage of the cell drops to zero
(d) The resistance of the circuit becomes zero
questions.answer: (a) An air gap is introduced, breaking the loop so zero current can flow
questions.explanation: Air has high resistance ($> 10^{14}\ \Omega$). Opening the switch creates an air gap that breaks continuity, stopping current.

questions.question: Why are copper and aluminium metals universally chosen for transmission cables and household wiring?
options: (b) They have very low electrical resistivity and conduct current efficiently
(c) They produce large amounts of heat
questions.answer: (b) They have very low electrical resistivity and conduct current efficiently
questions.explanation: Copper and aluminium have low electrical resistance, minimizing energy loss ($I^2R$) during transmission.

questions.question: Why are electrical tools (pliers, screwdrivers) equipped with thick plastic or rubber handles?
options: (b) Plastic and rubber are insulators that protect the electrician from electric shocks
(d) To increase the weight of the tool
questions.answer: (b) Plastic and rubber are insulators that protect the electrician from electric shocks
questions.explanation: Insulating handles prevent electric current from flowing through the user's body if the tool touches a live conductor.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the operation of a switch?
options: (a) It generates electric current in the circuit
(b) It closes (completes) or opens (breaks) the conducting path
(d) It steps up the potential difference
questions.answer: (b) It closes (completes) or opens (breaks) the conducting path
questions.explanation: A switch simply bridges or severs the electrical contacts, permitting or preventing the flow of charges.

questions.question: The work done in moving a 10 C charge between two points in a circuit is 350 J. What is the potential difference between the points?
questions.explanation: Potential difference $V = W/Q = 350\text{ J} / 10\text{ C} = 35\text{ V}$.

questions.question: Given that the elementary charge of an electron is $1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, how many electrons pass through a cross-section of wire per second when it carries 1 Ampere?
questions.explanation: $I = Q/t = n e / t \implies n = 1\text{ A} \times 1\text{ s} / (1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}) = 6.25 \times 10^{18}\text{ electrons}$.

questions.question: To connect multiple cells in series to form a battery, how must their terminals be arranged?
options: (a) Positive terminal of one cell connected to the negative terminal of the next
(b) Positive to positive and negative to negative
(c) Negative terminal of all cells to ground
questions.answer: (a) Positive terminal of one cell connected to the negative terminal of the next
questions.explanation: In series aiding connection, the positive terminal of each cell connects to the negative terminal of the following cell so their voltages add together.

questions.question: Statement 1: In an electric cell, chemical reactions produce potential difference between terminals. Statement 2: Two or more cells connected properly form a battery.
questions.explanation: A cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy, and a combination of two or more cells connected in series or parallel is defined as a battery.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: The filament in a modern incandescent lamp is made of which material?
questions.explanation: Tungsten has an exceptionally high melting point (~3422 °C) and high resistance, allowing it to become white hot without melting.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of incandescent lamps?
options: (b) They have a very short lifespan and low efficiency
questions.explanation: Incandescent lamps waste more than 90% of electrical energy as heat rather than visible light, giving them low energy efficiency and shorter operating lifespans.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: An incandescent lamp is a type of:
questions.explanation: A traditional glass bulb containing a coiled wire filament that glows upon heating is an incandescent lamp (electric bulb).

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: The thin wire inside an electric bulb which glows when electric current is passed through it is called the:
questions.explanation: The glowing element inside a bulb is called the filament, supported by two thick lead-in wires.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: An LED lamp works on the principle of converting electrical energy into:
questions.explanation: Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) emit light via electroluminescence at a p-n semiconductor junction, converting electricity directly to light with negligible heat loss.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: The bulb in an electric circuit glows primarily because of the:
questions.explanation: Electric current encounters high resistance in the tungsten filament, dissipating energy as heat ($H = I^2Rt$) until it reaches incandescence and emits light.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: An electric room heater is used to convert electrical energy primarily into:
questions.explanation: Electric room heaters use nichrome coils possessing high resistivity to convert electrical energy directly into thermal/heat energy.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: Statement 1: An electric bulb works on the heating effect of current. Statement 2: When current passes through the thin tungsten filament, it reaches high temperature and emits white light.
options: (a) Both statements are true and Statement 2 is the correct explanation of Statement 1
(b) Both statements are true but Statement 2 is not the correct explanation
(c) Statement 1 is true but Statement 2 is false
(d) Statement 1 is false but Statement 2 is true
questions.answer: (a) Both statements are true and Statement 2 is the correct explanation of Statement 1
questions.explanation: The filament's high resistance dissipates electrical energy into thermal energy ($I^2Rt$), heating it to ~2500 °C where it glows incandescently.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: In which of the following conditions will the amount of heat produced in a current-carrying wire increase? (i) Increasing current, (ii) Increasing wire resistance, (iii) Passing current for longer time.
questions.explanation: By Joule's Law of Heating, $H = I^2 R t$. Heat is directly proportional to the square of current, resistance, and time of flow.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: How does the electrical resistance of an ideal metallic (ohmic) conductor depend on the applied voltage at a constant temperature?
options: (d) Proportional to the square of voltage
questions.explanation: By Ohm's law, resistance $R = V/I$ is a constant property of the conductor's geometry and material, independent of applied voltage.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: As the operating temperature of an incandescent bulb's tungsten filament increases, what happens to its visible light emission?
questions.explanation: By Planck and Stefan-Boltzmann radiation laws, total radiant power scales as $T^4$, rapidly increasing the proportion of visible light emitted.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: Why does an LED bulb consume substantially less power than an incandescent bulb of equal luminosity?
options: (b) It converts electrical energy directly to photon emission with minimal thermal dissipation
questions.answer: (b) It converts electrical energy directly to photon emission with minimal thermal dissipation
questions.explanation: LEDs convert over 80% of electrical energy directly into light without needing to heat a wire to white-hot incandescence.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: A heating wire is glowing red hot. To further increase its temperature, what adjustment should be made?
options: (a) Increase the electric current flowing through the wire
(b) Decrease the voltage across the wire
(c) Dip the wire in cold water
questions.answer: (a) Increase the electric current flowing through the wire
questions.explanation: Rate of heat dissipation is $H = I^2Rt$. Increasing the current dramatically increases thermal energy generation.

questions.question: The safety device used to prevent the flow of excess current and protect household circuits is called a:
questions.explanation: An electric fuse contains a wire with a low melting point that melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds a safe threshold.

questions.question: Mark out the correct statement regarding safety devices:
options: (a) Both Fuses and MCBs are electrical safety devices
(b) Fuses are safety devices but MCBs are not
(c) MCBs are safety devices but fuses are not
(d) Neither fuses nor MCBs are safety devices
questions.answer: (a) Both Fuses and MCBs are electrical safety devices
questions.explanation: Both fuses (using thermal melting) and Miniature Circuit Breakers (MCBs, using electromagnetic trip mechanisms) protect circuits from overcurrent.

questions.question: The necessary requirement for an electric fuse wire is that it should be a:
options: (a) Conductor with a low melting point
(b) Conductor with a high melting point
(c) Insulator with a low melting point
(d) Insulator with a high melting point
questions.answer: (a) Conductor with a low melting point
questions.explanation: A fuse must conduct normal operating currents, but rapidly melt and sever the connection when an overcurrent heats it beyond its low melting point.

questions.question: Which certification mark is necessary on electrical appliances in India to ensure safety and quality standards?
questions.explanation: The ISI mark (issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards - BIS) certifies that an electrical appliance conforms to rigorous safety specifications.

questions.question: Which phenomenon occurs when the live wire and neutral wire come in direct contact with each other?
questions.explanation: When live and neutral wires touch with zero load resistance, circuit resistance drops near zero, causing a massive surge of current known as a short circuit.

questions.question: Choose the statement which is INCORRECT regarding an electric fuse:
options: (a) Fuses are safety devices inserted in all building circuits
(b) There is a safe maximum limit on current for every fuse
(c) If current exceeds the limit, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit
(d) A thick copper wire can safely be used as a replacement fuse wire
questions.answer: (d) A thick copper wire can safely be used as a replacement fuse wire
questions.explanation: Thick copper wire has a high melting point (~10⁸5 °C) and will not melt during overcurrent, defeating the safety purpose and risking fire.

questions.question: A torch bulb rated for 4.5 V is connected directly across a 9 V battery. What will happen to the bulb?
options: (a) It will glow with normal brightness
(b) It will glow very brightly for a brief moment and then burn out (fuse)
(c) It will not glow at all
questions.answer: (b) It will glow very brightly for a brief moment and then burn out (fuse)
questions.explanation: Applying double the rated voltage causes excess current to flow, overheating the filament beyond its melting point and burning it out.

questions.question: Which of the following is an UNSAFE practice that must NEVER be done with domestic electricity?
options: (a) Operating switches with wet hands or standing barefoot on a damp floor
(c) Replacing a blown fuse with the correct rated wire
(d) Turning off the main switch before changing a bulb
questions.answer: (a) Operating switches with wet hands or standing barefoot on a damp floor
questions.explanation: Water containing dissolved salts is conductive. Wet skin drastically reduces body resistance, causing electric shock.

questions.question: A conductor is connected across a constant voltage source. If its resistance is reduced to one-fourth ($R/4$), the current flowing through it will become:
questions.explanation: From Ohm's law $I = V/R$. If $R' = R/4$, then $I' = V / (R/4) = 4(V/R) = 4I$.

questions.question: The magnetic effect of electric current was discovered in 1820 by:
questions.explanation: Hans Christian Oersted observed that a magnetic compass needle deflected whenever placed near a wire carrying electric current.

questions.question: If you place a magnetic compass near a current-carrying wire, the needle will:
questions.explanation: A current-carrying wire generates an external magnetic field that exerts magnetic torque on the compass needle, deflecting it.

questions.question: A coil of insulated wire wrapped around a piece of soft iron carrying current becomes:
questions.explanation: Passing current through a solenoid wrapped on a soft iron core creates a temporary, strong magnet called an electromagnet.

questions.question: Soft iron is used as the core of an electromagnet instead of steel because:
options: (a) Soft iron is cheap and easily available
(b) Soft iron is a good conductor of electricity
(c) Soft iron loses its magnetism rapidly when current is switched off
questions.answer: (c) Soft iron loses its magnetism rapidly when current is switched off
questions.explanation: Soft iron has low magnetic retentivity (coercivity). It becomes strongly magnetized with current, and instantly demagnetizes when current stops.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding an electromagnet is FALSE?
options: (a) Insulated wire is wound around its core
(b) It functions only when current is flowing
(c) Its magnetic polarity can be reversed by reversing current
(d) It is a permanent magnet that cannot be turned off
questions.answer: (d) It is a permanent magnet that cannot be turned off
questions.explanation: Electromagnets are temporary magnets whose magnetic field can be easily turned on, turned off, or varied in strength.

questions.question: A traditional electric door bell makes use of which type of electromagnet?
questions.explanation: A U-shaped (horseshoe) electromagnet brings both magnetic poles close to a soft iron armature, providing strong attraction to strike the gong.

questions.question: The magnetic strength of an electromagnet does NOT depend upon:
options: (a) The magnitude of current flowing through the coil
(b) The number of turns in the coil
(c) The color or material of the outer wire insulation
(d) The nature of the magnetic core material
questions.answer: (c) The color or material of the outer wire insulation
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic field strength depends on $B = \mu n I$ (core permeability, turns per unit length, and current). The insulation color has zero physical effect.

questions.question: When the direction of electric current flowing through a straight conductor is reversed, the deflection of a nearby magnetic compass needle:
options: (a) Remains in the exact same direction
questions.explanation: By Ampère's Right-Hand Grip Rule, reversing current reverses the magnetic field lines around the wire, flipping the deflection direction.

questions.question: When an unmagnetized soft iron rod is brought near either pole of a magnetic compass needle, what happens?
options: (a) Only the North pole is attracted
(b) Only the South pole is attracted
(c) Both poles are attracted to the iron rod
(d) Both poles are repelled by the iron rod
questions.answer: (c) Both poles are attracted to the iron rod
questions.explanation: Magnetic induction creates opposite poles in unmagnetized soft iron. Therefore, either pole of a permanent magnet attracts unmagnetized iron.

questions.question: Which coil produces the strongest electromagnet for a given flow of electric current?
questions.explanation: Magnetic field strength is proportional to turn density $n = N/L$. For coil B: $n = 200/5 = 40\text{ turns/cm}$, which is the highest turn density.

questions.question: A straight horizontal copper wire placed over and parallel to a compass needle carries current from South to North. The North pole of the needle deflects towards:
questions.explanation: By the SNOW rule: Current flowing from South to North Over a compass needle deflects the North pole towards West.

questions.question: In an experiment, electromagnet X with 60 turns attracted 25 iron pins, while electromagnet Y with 20 turns attracted 8 pins using the same battery. This proves:
options: (a) Strength of an electromagnet increases with the number of turns of wire
(c) Turns have no effect on magnetic field
questions.answer: (a) Strength of an electromagnet increases with the number of turns of wire
questions.explanation: Each turn adds its own magnetic field to the solenoid. Increasing turns directly increases the total magnetic field ($B \propto N$).

questions.question: When a magnetic compass needle is brought near a current-carrying straight wire: (I) the needle deflects, (II) the needle aligns tangentially to concentric magnetic field lines around the wire. Which is true?
questions.explanation: The magnetic field around a straight conductor consists of concentric circles; the compass aligns along these circular field lines.

questions.question: In which arrangement will a bulb glow? (I) Terminals connected across a complete loop to cell (+) and (-), (II) Only one terminal connected, (III) Filament broken, (IV) Plastic wire used.
questions.explanation: A bulb requires an intact filament and a complete continuous metallic conducting loop connected across both terminals of the cell.

questions.question: If the positive and negative terminals of a dry cell are connected directly by a thick copper wire with no appliance in between:
options: (a) The cell will store extra charge
(c) A short circuit occurs; large current flows, the cell heats up and discharges rapidly
(d) The voltage of the cell increases
questions.answer: (c) A short circuit occurs; large current flows, the cell heats up and discharges rapidly
questions.explanation: Direct connection without load creates a short circuit. The chemical energy is rapidly depleted as internal heat, ruining the cell.

questions.question: Which of the following schematic representations shows the correct series combination of three cells in a battery?
questions.explanation: In a proper series battery connection, the negative terminal of each cell joins the positive terminal of the next, producing $V_{total} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$.

questions.question: Why are the two lead-in wires connecting the filament of a bulb insulated or spaced apart so they do not touch each other inside the bulb?
options: (b) Touching would short-circuit the filament, bypassing it so the bulb would not glow
(c) To keep the bulb light in weight
questions.answer: (b) Touching would short-circuit the filament, bypassing it so the bulb would not glow
questions.explanation: If the lead-in wires touch below the filament, current takes the zero-resistance path, bypassing the filament completely.

questions.question: Which practical test proves that an electromagnet has been successfully activated?
options: (b) It attracts steel paper clips or iron filings when current flows, and drops them when switched off
(c) It changes color from red to blue
questions.answer: (b) It attracts steel paper clips or iron filings when current flows, and drops them when switched off
questions.explanation: Ferromagnetic materials like iron clips are attracted to magnetic poles. Losing attraction when current stops proves it is an electromagnet.

questions.question: Which scenario represents a dangerous 'short circuit' in a household installation?
options: (a) Turning on a ceiling fan and a television simultaneously
(b) Connecting a high-power geyser to a 15 A socket
(c) Accidental direct contact between bare live and neutral wires without any appliance resistance
(d) Switching off the main circuit breaker
questions.answer: (c) Accidental direct contact between bare live and neutral wires without any appliance resistance
questions.explanation: Direct contact between live and neutral wires reduces circuit impedance to near zero, causing dangerous overcurrent that can ignite insulation.

questions.question: Match Column I with Column II: (P) Filament material, (Q) Household safety fuse, (R) Electromagnet core, (S) Connecting wires. (1) Soft iron, (2) Tungsten, (3) Copper, (4) Lead-tin alloy.
questions.explanation: Filament = Tungsten (2); Fuse = Lead-tin alloy (4); Electromagnet core = Soft iron (1); Connecting wires = Copper (3).

questions.question: Ramesh wants to double the lifting strength of his lab electromagnet. Which combined actions will achieve this?
options: (a) Increase the number of turns in the coil and increase the current flowing through it
(b) Decrease the number of turns and use a plastic core
questions.answer: (a) Increase the number of turns in the coil and increase the current flowing through it
questions.explanation: Electromagnet strength depends directly on ampere-turns ($N \times I$) and core permeability. Increasing turns and current increases magnetic flux.

questions.question: In a testing circuit with three mystery rods (M1, M2, M3), inserting M1 causes the bulb to glow; M2 leaves it off; M3 causes it to glow brightly. Which identifies the materials?
options: (a) M1: Glass, M2: Copper, M3: Wood
(b) M1: Iron, M2: Plastic, M3: Silver
(c) M1: Rubber, M2: Aluminium, M3: Plastic
(d) M1: Wood, M2: Glass, M3: Rubber
questions.answer: (b) M1: Iron, M2: Plastic, M3: Silver
questions.explanation: M1 (Iron) conducts current; M2 (Plastic) is an insulator; M3 (Silver) is the best conductor, producing a bright glow.

questions.question: Match Column I with Column II: (P) Electric cell, (Q) Electric switch, (R) Electromagnet, (S) Electric fuse. (1) Breaks or completes circuit, (2) Produces electricity from chemicals, (3) Melts on excessive current, (4) Coil behaving as magnet.
questions.explanation: Cell = Produces electricity (2); Switch = Makes/breaks circuit (1); Electromagnet = Coil magnet (4); Fuse = Melts on excess current (3).

questions.question: Three identical bulbs X, Y, and Z are connected in series with a battery and a switch. When the switch is closed, in what order do they light up?
options: (a) Bulb X first, then Y, then Z
(b) Bulb Z first, then Y, then X
questions.explanation: The electric field propagates through the circuit near the speed of light ($~3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$). Electrons everywhere drift simultaneously, lighting all series bulbs at the same instant.

questions.question: If 5 Coulombs of electric charge flows through a conductor in 2 seconds, how many electrons flow through the conductor per second?
questions.explanation: Current $I = Q/t = 5\text{ C} / 2\text{ s} = 2.5\text{ A}$. Number of electrons per second $n/t = I/e = 2.5 / (1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 1.5625 \times 10^{19}$.

questions.question: Five identical bulbs are connected across two dry cells: Bulbs 1, 2, 3, 4 are in parallel, and Bulb 5 is in the main series branch. If Bulb 2 burns out, what happens to the remaining bulbs?
questions.explanation: In parallel branches, burning out one branch does not break the circuit for the parallel companion branches or the main line.

questions.question: Compare four electromagnets: (I) 10 turns, 4 A; (II) 10 turns, 2 A; (III) 20 turns, 4 A; (IV) 20 turns, 2 A. Which one produces the strongest magnetic field?
questions.explanation: Magnetomotive force is proportional to ampere-turns ($N \times I$): Coil III has $20 \times 4 = 80\text{ A}\cdot\text{turns}$, the highest of all four.

questions.question: Using the Right-Hand Grip Rule for a solenoid: If current viewed from one end flows clockwise, that end behaves as a:
questions.explanation: By the Clock Rule: Clockwise current corresponds to a South magnetic pole (S); Counter-clockwise current corresponds to a North magnetic pole (N).

questions.question: In a circuit where switch S1 is in the main line and switches S2 and S3 are in parallel branch lines to a lamp, the lamp will glow when:
options: (a) S1 is closed and either S2 or S3 is closed
(b) S1 is open and S2 is closed
(d) S1 is closed and both S2 and S3 are open
questions.answer: (a) S1 is closed and either S2 or S3 is closed
questions.explanation: S1 must be closed to power the main supply, and at least one parallel branch switch (S2 or S3) must be closed to complete the loop to the lamp.

questions.question: An electric kettle is rated '500 W, 220 V'. What does this specification indicate?
options: (a) It produces 500 Joules of heat energy per second when connected across 220 Volts
questions.answer: (a) It produces 500 Joules of heat energy per second when connected across 220 Volts
questions.explanation: A power rating of 500 W means the appliance converts electrical energy into thermal energy at the rate of 500 Joules per second when powered at 220 V.

questions.question: Four circuits are powered by identical 1.5 V cells: (i) 1 cell, (ii) 2 cells in series, (iii) 3 cells in series, (iv) 4 cells in series. The bulb voltage is highest in:
questions.explanation: In series aiding connection, voltages sum up: Circuit (iv) provides $4 \times 1.5\text{ V} = 6.0\text{ V}$, yielding the greatest potential difference.

questions.question: A student tests objects in three containers: C1 (copper coin, steel nail), C2 (plastic toy, rubber band), C3 (aluminium clip, graphite pencil lead). In which containers are ALL objects conductors?
questions.explanation: C1 (copper and steel) and C3 (aluminium and graphite) are all electrical conductors. Plastic and rubber in C2 are insulators.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT? (i) The human body is an electrical insulator, (ii) Pure distilled water is an insulator, but tap water conducts electricity, (iii) Air is normally an insulator.
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is incorrect: the human body contains ionized water and is a conductor of electricity (which is why humans can experience electric shocks).

questions.question: The combination of two or more cells connected in series is called a _______.
questions.explanation: In a battery, the positive terminal of one cell is connected to the negative terminal of the next.

questions.question: The bulb will glow in a circuit only when the switch is in the _______ position.
questions.explanation: A closed switch completes the conducting loop, allowing continuous electron flow.

questions.question: The switch in a circuit is used to control whether the circuit is _______ or _______.
questions.explanation: Opening the switch introduces an air gap of infinite resistance, stopping current.

questions.question: A thin coiled wire inside an electric lamp that glows white-hot when current passes through it is called the _______.
questions.explanation: Tungsten filaments possess high melting points (~3422°C) allowing incandescence without melting.

questions.question: An electric _______ is a continuous unbroken pathway for electric current to pass through.
questions.explanation: Current requires a closed continuous conducting loop from positive to negative terminal.

questions.question: The top metal cap of a standard dry cell is its _______ terminal.
questions.explanation: The metal cap connects to the carbon rod cathode (+), while the zinc bottom case is the anode (−).

questions.question: If the switch is placed in the _______ position, current ceases and the bulb will not glow.
questions.explanation: An open switch breaks circuit continuity.

questions.question: In the standard electrical symbol for a cell, the longer thinner vertical line represents the _______ terminal.
questions.explanation: The longer line denotes high electric potential (+), while the shorter thick line denotes low potential (−).

questions.question: When electric current is switched on in a room heater, its coiled heating element becomes _______ and emits radiant heat.
questions.explanation: Joule heating (H = I²Rt) elevates the nichrome coil temperature until it glows red.

questions.question: A safety device based on the thermal heating effect of current that melts during overloading is called a _______.
questions.explanation: The low melting point alloy wire melts when current exceeds rated amperage, protecting wiring.

questions.question: An insulator does not allow electric current to pass through it under normal conditions.
questions.explanation: Insulators have bound valence electrons and lack free charge carriers.

questions.question: Electric current flows only when a circuit forms a complete, unbroken closed loop.
questions.explanation: Charge cannot bridge open physical air gaps in low-voltage DC circuits.

questions.question: A lamp with a broken filament is called a fused lamp and cannot glow.
questions.explanation: A severed filament breaks circuit continuity across the bulb terminals.

questions.question: An electric switch in the 'OFF' position facilitates the flow of electric current.
questions.explanation: An open switch breaks the conducting path, completely halting current flow.

questions.question: To make a battery of two cells, the negative terminal of one cell must connect to the negative terminal of the second cell.
questions.explanation: Cells in series must connect negative terminal to positive terminal (+ to −).

questions.question: When current through a fuse exceeds its safe rated limit, the fuse wire melts and opens the circuit.
questions.explanation: Joule heating melts the low-melting-point alloy, averting electrical fire hazards.

questions.question: An electromagnet behaves as a permanent magnet even after current is turned off.
questions.explanation: Electromagnets lose virtually all magnetic power immediately when current stops (temporary magnet).

questions.question: An electric bell operates using the magnetic attraction of an electromagnet on a soft iron armature.
questions.explanation: The electromagnet repeatedly pulls the hammer against the gong and breaks contact in an oscillating cycle.

questions.question: A Miniature Circuit Breaker (MCB) can automatically trip and protect household circuits without requiring wire replacement.
questions.explanation: MCBs trip automatically during overcurrent and can simply be reset by flipping the lever.

questions.question: Insulating materials like PVC rubber are wrapped around copper wires to prevent short circuits and electrical shocks.
questions.explanation: High dielectric strength materials prevent dangerous current leakage and accidental electrocution.

questions.question: Draw in your notebook the symbols to represent the following components of electrical circuits: connecting wires, switch in the 'OFF' position, bulb, cell, switch in the 'ON' position, and battery.
questions.answer: Standard Schematic Symbols:Connecting wire: A straight plain continuous line.Switch in OFF position: An open gap line with an inclined bar.Bulb: A circle enclosing a looped filament coil.Electric cell: One long thin vertical line (positive terminal) paired with a parallel short thick vertical line (negative terminal).Switch in ON position: Continuous straight line with dots bridged.Battery: Combination of alternating long thin and short thick lines connected in series (+ to -).
questions.explanation: Official textbook model solution and marking rubric breakdown.

questions.question: Why is a switch placed anywhere in a circuit able to control the bulb?
questions.answer: An electric current requires an unbroken, closed conducting loop to flow from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the cell. If the switch is opened (OFF) at any point in the circuit, the conductive loop is broken (open circuit), halting the flow of electrons through all components immediately.
questions.explanation: Official textbook model solution and marking rubric breakdown.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: Explain why the filament of an electric bulb glows white-hot while the connecting wires remain cool.
questions.answer: The filament is fabricated from tungsten, which possesses extremely high electrical resistance and an ultra-high melting point (approx. $3422^\circ\text{C}$). When current passes through, the high resistance causes intense Joule heating ($H = I^2Rt$), heating it to white incandescence ($~2500^\circ\text{C}$) to emit visible light.In contrast, connecting wires are composed of thick copper or aluminium with negligible electrical resistance, so heat dissipation is imperceptibly small.
questions.explanation: Official textbook model solution and marking rubric breakdown.

questions.topic: Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law
questions.question: Name two devices that deliberately utilize the heating effect of electric current, and state the material used for their heating elements.
questions.answer: Devices: Electric iron, electric toaster, geyser, room heater.Material: Nichrome (an alloy of nickel, chromium, and iron) because of its exceptionally high resistivity and high resistance to oxidation (does not burn or melt easily at high temperatures).
questions.explanation: Official textbook model solution and marking rubric breakdown.

questions.question: Explain the working principle and construction of an electric fuse. Why should a thick copper wire never be used as a fuse wire?
questions.answer: An electric fuse is a critical safety device designed to break the circuit in the event of excessive current (overloading or short-circuiting). It consists of a thin alloy wire (typically tin-lead alloy) with a low melting point.When current exceeds the safe limit, the Joule heat generated ($I^2Rt$) rapidly raises the temperature past the alloy's melting point, causing the wire to melt and break the circuit safely.Why copper wire must NOT be used: Copper has very low resistance and a very high melting point ($10⁸5^\circ\text{C}$). It will not melt during dangerous current spikes, allowing the excessive current to overheat house wiring and cause catastrophic electrical fires.
questions.explanation: Official textbook model solution and marking rubric breakdown.

questions.question: What is a Miniature Circuit Breaker (MCB), and what advantage does it offer over traditional wire fuses?
questions.answer: An MCB is an automatic electromagnetic switch that automatically trips into the 'OFF' position whenever current exceeds safe thresholds. Unlike traditional fuses that require manual replacement of melted wires, an MCB can be simply reset back to the 'ON' position once the electrical fault is corrected.
questions.explanation: Official textbook model solution and marking rubric breakdown.

questions.question: Describe Oersted's experiment and state its fundamental scientific conclusion.
questions.answer: In 1820, Danish scientist Hans Christian Oersted placed a magnetic compass needle parallel and close to a straight conducting wire. When electric current was switched ON, the compass needle immediately deflected from its North-South alignment. When the current was reversed, the needle deflected in the opposite direction. When current was switched OFF, the needle returned to magnetic North.Conclusion: An electric current flowing through a conductor generates a surrounding magnetic field.
questions.explanation: Official textbook model solution and marking rubric breakdown.

questions.question: Explain the working mechanism of an electric bell with a circuit schematic description.
questions.answer: An electric bell operates via an electromagnet and a make-and-break contact mechanism:When the bell switch is pressed, current flows through the electromagnet coil, magnetizing its soft iron core.The energized electromagnet attracts the soft iron armature attached to a spring strip.As the armature rushes toward the electromagnet, the striker hits the metallic gong, producing a loud ring.However, this forward motion simultaneously pulls the contact screw away from the contact strip, breaking the circuit.With the circuit broken, current stops, the electromagnet de-energizes, and the spring pulls the armature back.As the armature springs back, it touches the contact screw again, completing the circuit once more. This rapid make-and-break cycle repeats continuously as long as the switch is held down.
questions.explanation: Official textbook model solution and marking rubric breakdown.

questions.question: HOTS Q1: Four identical bulbs A, B, C, and D are connected in a circuit. Bulbs A and B are in series, and this combination is connected in parallel with bulb C. Bulb D is connected in the main line. If bulb C's filament breaks, explain what happens to the brightness of bulbs A, B, and D.
questions.answer: Circuit Analysis:Total circuit current flows through main-line bulb D before splitting into parallel branches $(A+B)$ and $C$.When bulb C burns out, branch C becomes an open circuit.The total equivalent resistance of the entire circuit increases because the parallel path has been removed.Due to the increased total resistance, the total current drawn from the battery decreases. Hence, bulb D in the main line dims slightly.However, the voltage across the surviving branch $(A+B)$ increases because the voltage drop across D has decreased. Therefore, bulbs A and B actually glow brighter than before!
questions.explanation: Official textbook model solution and marking rubric breakdown.

questions.question: HOTS Q2: Why are LEDs (Light Emitting Diodes) increasingly replacing incandescent bulbs and CFLs? State two major technical advantages.
questions.answer: Advantages of LEDs:High Energy Efficiency: LEDs produce light via electroluminescence (electron-hole recombination in semiconductors) without wasting massive energy as heat ($>80\%$ less energy consumed than incandescent bulbs).Long Lifespan & Durability: LEDs have no fragile filament to break or burn out, operating for 25,000 to 50,000 hours with negligible heat dissipation.
questions.explanation: Official textbook model solution and marking rubric breakdown.
